past_medical_history: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (well controlled on insulin pump)
No prior neuromuscular or autoimmune disease besides DM1

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented. Normal cognition and language.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis, right greater than left. Levator excursion right 6mm, left 10mm. Complete fatigable ptosis right eye on sustained upgaze at 38 seconds. Horizontal diplopia on leftward gaze. Right eye adduction weakness. Pupils equal, reactive. No proptosis. Facial weakness bilateral.
neurological_exam.motor: Deltoids 4-/5. Hip flexors 4/5. Neck flexors 4-/5. Distal 5/5. Clear fatigability on sustained arm elevation and neck flexion.
neurological_exam.additional: Voice nasal after 3 minutes speech. Mild dysphagia — pills difficult to swallow. NIF -60 cmH2O. No respiratory distress. Patient noted: as a pharmacist she recognized fatigability as potentially NMJ-related and specifically requested MG workup.

patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and swallowing difficulty for 10 weeks
patient.history_present_illness: A 45-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus managed with an insulin pump presented with 10 weeks of bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and dysphagia. She works as a pharmacist and described noticing her right eyelid drooping approximately 10 weeks ago. She recognized the diurnal variation (consistently worse at the end of her 10-hour pharmacy shifts, better after a night's sleep) as potentially significant and began researching myasthenia gravis. She developed horizontal double vision on looking to the left approximately 7 weeks ago, with the images side by side and worsening with sustained left lateral gaze. She has had difficulty swallowing pills over the past 4 weeks — she has to swallow each pill separately with a large quantity of water and cannot take the multiple tablets she used to take all at once. She reports that her voice becomes nasal and that patients at the pharmacy have commented that her speech sounds different in the afternoon. She has had proximal arm weakness — she asked her colleague to help her reach upper pharmacy shelves because her arms tire out overhead. She denies sensory symptoms, no headache, no neck pain, no limb weakness at rest. Her type 1 diabetes is very well controlled with her insulin pump (HbA1c 6.6%). She specifically requested that her primary care physician order anti-AChR antibodies, which came back from outside laboratory as 'reported as borderline positive.' She was then referred urgently to neurology. Her family history includes paternal type 1 diabetes; she was not aware of MG in her family. She has not had any recent infections, new medications, or stressful events beyond her normal busy work schedule.

findings.result: Marked improvement in ptosis within 60 seconds of edrophonium — ptosis reduced from complete to minimal
findings.significance: Positive pharmacological response — marked improvement in ptosis following edrophonium administration
Normal motor and sensory conduction; normal baseline CMAP amplitudes

specialized_test.impression: Clearly abnormal RNS with 17–20% decremental responses at deltoid and nasalis. Positive edrophonium (Tensilon) test with marked improvement in ptosis. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission

labs.interpretation: Anti-AChR binding antibody markedly elevated at 5.8 nmol/L (reference <0.5 nmol/L). Anti-AChR blocking and modulating antibodies also elevated. Anti-MuSK negative. Anti-titin negative. Anti-GAD65 antibody markedly elevated (>2000 IU/mL; reference <5 IU/mL). Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are found in a subset of patients with neuromuscular junction disorders; elevated results are associated with autoimmune neuromuscular junction disease
abnormal_values_summary: Anti-AChR binding 5.8 nmol/L (markedly elevated; ref <0.5 nmol/L)

findings.description: No anterior mediastinal mass. Residual thymic tissue with fatty involution appropriate for age 45. No lymphadenopathy. No thymoma identified.

ct.impression: No anterior mediastinal mass identified. Residual thymic tissue with fatty involution appropriate for age. No lymphadenopathy. Lungs clear

output.impression: Markedly abnormal SFEMG with increased jitter (mean MCD 71 µs) and high blocking rate (75%). Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission

output.proposed: Prednisone 15-20mg daily for MG in Type 1 diabetic on insulin pump
interactions: Prednisone + insulin pump: corticosteroids cause significant insulin resistance and hyperglycemia — pump settings will need adjustment
Expected glucose impact: typically requires 20-50% increase in basal rate and correction bolus increases
warnings: Consult endocrinology for insulin pump adjustment protocol during corticosteroid initiation
Patient (pharmacist) may already have understanding of this interaction — engage her knowledge
Start glucose monitoring 4x daily minimum during steroid initiation
Steroid-induced hyperglycemia typically peaks 4-8 hours after prednisone dose
alternatives: Azathioprine as steroid-sparing to minimize prednisone exposure in T1DM

findings.description: No anterior mediastinal mass on repeat contrast CT. Fatty thymus only.

output.impression: No anterior mediastinal mass on contrast-enhanced CT chest. Fatty thymus only. No lymphadenopathy

output.proposed: Pyridostigmine 60mg q4-6h in patient with codeine allergy (nausea)
interactions: Pyridostigmine cholinergic side effects include nausea, abdominal cramps, diarrhea — may be bothersome given patient's gastrointestinal sensitivity with codeine allergy (nausea reaction)
Pyridostigmine is not opioid — codeine allergy does not affect pyridostigmine; separate mechanism
warnings: Codeine allergy (nausea) does not contraindicate pyridostigmine
Warn patient of GI side effects of pyridostigmine — nausea, cramping; start low (30-45mg q6h) and titrate
Glycopyrrolate 1mg TID may reduce cholinergic GI side effects if needed

output.query: Thymectomy myasthenia gravis MGTX trial non-thymomatous AChR positive

results.title: MGTX Trial: Randomized Thymectomy in Myasthenia Gravis
results.finding: Thymectomy + prednisone superior to prednisone alone in AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65; lower QMG scores, lower prednisone requirements, higher remission rates at 3 years; thymectomy recommended regardless of CT chest

results.title: Laparoscopic vs robotic thymectomy for MG
results.finding: VATS and robotic approaches have equivalent outcomes to median sternotomy for non-invasive thymoma and thymic hyperplasia; shorter hospital stay, less pain

output.summary: MGTX trial (NEJM 2016) provides Class I evidence that thymectomy + prednisone is superior to prednisone alone in AChR antibody-positive generalized neuromuscular junction disease aged 18–65, regardless of CT chest findings. VATS and robotic approaches have equivalent outcomes to median sternotomy for non-invasive thymic pathology with shorter hospital stay.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), AChR antibody-positive, without thymoma; concurrent type 1 diabetes with markedly elevated anti-GAD65 (polyautoimmunity)

differential.key_features: Anti-GAD65 >2000 raises SPS possibility, but SPS causes rigidity with stimulus-sensitive spasms, not fatigable ptosis/diplopia; AChR antibodies confirm MG.
T1DM; cranial neuropathy is acute, painful, monocular; this is bilateral and fatigable.
Markedly positive AChR; baseline CMAPs normal.
Patient not on penicillamine or other MG-inducing agents.
Markedly positive AChR establishes organic pathology.

optimal_actions.action: Order serologies: anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4, and TSH/free-T4 for thyroid autoimmunity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AChR antibody positive; TSH evaluates for comorbid thyroid disease

optimal_actions.action: Order repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at 2-3 Hz across proximal and facial muscles
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Decrement >10% in symptomatic muscles supports postsynaptic NMJ disorder
Increased jitter and blocking on extensor digitorum communis or orbicularis oculi confirms NMJ transmission failure

optimal_actions.action: Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No thymoma; thymic involution appropriate for age

optimal_actions.action: Review MGFA classification and current treatment guidance (pyridostigmine, prednisone, steroid-sparing, IVIG/PLEX, thymectomy)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MGFA classification stages disease severity; thymectomy benefits AChR+ generalized MG (MGTX); IVIG/PLEX for crisis

tool_parameters.query: myasthenia gravis MGFA classification treatment thymectomy

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions for MG-exacerbating agents (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, procainamide)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Flag aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium, telithromycin, NMBs as contraindicated or use-with-caution in MG

optimal_actions.action: Bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) — repeat q4h in crisis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline FVC/NIF to assess crisis risk in patients with bulbar or limb involvement

optimal_actions.action: Bedside ice-pack test for ptosis (cheap, ~80% sensitive for ocular MG)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Improvement of ptosis after 2 minutes of cooling supports MG

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Brain MRI is non-contributory in typical MG; reserve for cases where an alternative CNS cause (brainstem lesion, demyelination) is genuinely in the differential.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; reserve single-fiber EMG for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases (resource stewardship).

critical_actions: CT chest — required in all confirmed MG (here negative)
Single-fiber EMG given diagnostic clarity already achieved
Coordinate steroid plan with diabetes team — insulin pump adjustment for steroid-induced hyperglycemia
Investigate anti-GAD65 — exclude stiff-person syndrome (clinically incompatible here)
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
T1DM + MG is classic polyautoimmunity; anti-GAD65 in this context most often relates to T1DM, not SPS.
Steroid initiation requires anticipatory insulin dose adjustment.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue stiff-person syndrome workup; miss MG diagnosis.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Anti-GAD65 is elevated in 80% of T1DM and does not, by itself, indicate SPS; the AChR-antibody titer and RNS decrement are diagnostic of MG.
